cases.title: Children's online privacy regulation (COPPA amended rule)

business_activity.name: Family of Apps services used by minors

cases.policy_mechanism: Product requirement and compliance rule: amended COPPA Rule (16 CFR 312) tightening consent, data retention, and safe-harbor obligations for online services directed at children

mechanism_chain.text: The FTC amended the COPPA Rule with an effective date of June 23, 2025 and a compliance date of April 22, 2026 for most provisions.

The amended rule could require changes to how Meta's services handle users under 13 and how parental consent and data retention operate, which could alter product design and data practices in Family of Apps.
The scale depends on how many Meta users are children covered by COPPA and on enforcement posture; Meta does not disclose minor-user revenue, so product-level financial exposure is unknown.

events.description: FTC publishes amended COPPA Rule in the Federal Register (90 FR, final rule)
Amended rule effective
General compliance date for regulated entities
Meta FY2025 10-K discloses an FTC proceeding alleging COPPA violations that 'seeks changes to our business'

financial_linkage.detail: Consolidated FY2025 revenue $201.0B (XBRL, company-wide). No product-level or age-cohort revenue is disclosed.
financial_linkage.gap: Product-level exposure for minors cannot be derived from consolidated or segment revenue - labeled Unknown per the financial linkage ladder.

cases.rationale: A final federal rule is past adoption and inside its compliance window, and Meta itself discloses a parallel FTC COPPA proceeding seeking business changes. Exposure is Meaningful rather than Core because the affected cohort (under-13 users) is a bounded subset of Family of Apps and Meta's own framing treats it as one of several regulatory pressures.
gaps: State-level age-verification and parental-consent laws (disclosed by Meta for Arkansas, California, Colorado, Florida, New York, Texas, Utah) are not yet connected as sources - patchwork risk is asserted by the company but not independently verified here.
No FTC enforcement docket connector; the parallel proceeding is evidenced only by company disclosure.

cases.title: FTC v. Meta structural antitrust litigation (Instagram / WhatsApp divestiture remedy sought)

business_activity.name: Instagram and WhatsApp within Family of Apps

cases.authority: Federal Trade Commission / US District Court for the District of Columbia
cases.policy_mechanism: Enforcement action with court remedy: permanent injunction and equitable relief including divestiture or reconstruction of Instagram and WhatsApp

mechanism_chain.text: The FTC filed a complaint in December 2020 alleging anticompetitive conduct including the Instagram (2012) and WhatsApp (2014) acquisitions.
The complaint seeks equitable relief including divestiture or reconstruction of Instagram and WhatsApp.
A structural remedy would separate core revenue-generating products from Meta; the CMA-ordered Giphy divestiture in 2023 shows such remedies are executed in practice.
Instagram-specific revenue is not disclosed, so the financial scale of a divestiture cannot be computed from public filings.

events.description: FTC files complaint in D.D.C. alleging Section 5 FTC Act / Section 2 Sherman Act violations
Precedent: Meta completes Giphy divestiture under UK CMA order
Meta FY2025 10-K continues to disclose the suit and the divestiture remedy sought

financial_linkage.detail: Instagram and WhatsApp results are reported only within the Family of Apps segment; no product-level revenue is disclosed.
financial_linkage.gap: Cannot assign product-level exposure from consolidated or segment revenue - Unknown on the financial linkage ladder.

cases.rationale: The remedy sought strikes at core business assets, which makes business exposure Core by construction. But the case rests entirely on company disclosure of the litigation; no court-docket connector exists in this build, so current procedural posture (post-trial status, remedy phase) is a material coverage gap. No outcome probability is claimed.
gaps: No court docket connector (PACER/D.D.C.) - the current litigation posture cannot be independently verified in this build.
Remedy scope and timing unknown; time horizon is Unclear by design.

cases.title: Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (IRA) - Ibrance maximum fair price

business_activity.name: Medicare Part D-covered prescription drugs, incl. Ibrance (palbociclib)

cases.authority: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), HHS
cases.policy_mechanism: Price setting: statutory negotiation program setting a maximum fair price (MFP) for selected Medicare Part D drugs; CMS publishes Ibrance (Pfizer Inc.) with an agreed negotiated price of $7,871 per 30-day supply effective January 1, 2027

mechanism_chain.text: The IRA Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program is operating: CMS issued final guidance for the second cycle and signed agreements with the manufacturers of all 15 selected drugs, including Pfizer Inc. for Ibrance.

CMS publishes an agreed negotiated price for Ibrance of $7,871 per 30-day supply for CY2027, a 50% discount from its 2024 list price of $15,741, effective January 1, 2027; Part D gross covered costs for Ibrance were $2.04B in CY2024 across 16,000 enrollees.

The negotiated price directly reduces Pfizer's realized US revenue per Ibrance unit dispensed under Medicare Part D from 2027; total company impact depends on Ibrance's Part D volume versus other channels and on portfolio breadth, which retrieved sources do not quantify.

CMS is already drafting guidance for manufacturer effectuation of maximum fair prices in 2028, so further Pfizer products could be selected in later cycles; no later-cycle Pfizer selection is in retrieved sources.

events.description: CMS announces final guidance for the second cycle of the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program and manufacturer effectuation of the maximum fair price in 2026 and 2027
HHS announces 15 additional drugs selected for the second cycle of Medicare drug price negotiation; Ibrance is on the list
CMS announces agreements signed with manufacturers of all 15 second-cycle drugs; table lists 'Ibrance | Pfizer Inc.'
Negotiated maximum fair prices for second-cycle drugs take effect; CMS lists Ibrance at $7,871 per 30-day supply (50% below 2024 list)
CMS publishes draft guidance for manufacturer effectuation of the maximum fair price in 2028; comments due September 18, 2026

financial_linkage.detail: CMS publishes Ibrance-specific figures: negotiated price $7,871 per 30-day supply (CY2027) vs $15,741 2024 list price (50% discount); $2,036,178,000 Part D gross covered prescription drug costs in CY2024; 16,000 Part D enrollees used the drug in CY2024. Consolidated FY2025 revenue $62.6B (SEC EDGAR XBRL us-gaap:Revenues, FY2025 10-K).
financial_linkage.gap: Part D gross covered cost is not Pfizer net revenue (rebates, channel mix, and non-Medicare sales are not in retrieved sources); Ibrance-level net impact cannot be computed from retrieved sources.

cases.rationale: This is a directly evidenced, product-level exposure: CMS names Pfizer Inc. as the participating manufacturer for Ibrance in the second negotiation cycle and publishes the agreed price, the 2024 list price, the discount, the Part D spend, and the enrollee count. Exposure is Meaningful rather than Core because the retrieved sources quantify one product's Medicare channel only; Pfizer's consolidated and segment revenue could not be retrieved (SEC EDGAR blocked from the build environment), so portfolio-level materiality is honestly unquantified.
gaps: SEC EDGAR 10-K full text for Pfizer not yet snapshotted in this build - company risk-factor disclosure on the negotiation program is pending, not absent. (EDGAR reachable via browser fetch; submissions and revenue concept retrieved.)
Senate LDA lobbying filings are likewise blocked (HTTP 403) - Pfizer advocacy on the IRA is not covered in this build.

cases.title: Federal worker classification rule under the FLSA (2024 rule vs. 2026 rescission proposal)

business_activity.name: Mobility and Delivery supply model using independent-contractor drivers and couriers

cases.authority: US Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
cases.policy_mechanism: Labor rule / interpretive standard: regulatory guidance determining employee vs. independent contractor status under the FLSA (29 CFR part 795)

mechanism_chain.text: A January 2024 DOL final rule set the current analysis for determining employee vs. independent contractor status under the FLSA.
In February 2026 DOL proposed to rescind the 2024 rule and readopt the January 2021 analysis with modifications.

Uber discloses that reclassification of drivers as employees would require it to fundamentally change its business model with adverse effect on results of operations, financial position and cash flows.

The direction of travel at the federal level is toward a more employer-favorable standard, but state and foreign classification regimes (which the 10-K emphasizes) are unaffected by the federal rescission.

events.description: DOL final rule: Employee or Independent Contractor Classification Under the FLSA (89 FR 1638)
DOL proposed rule to rescind the 2024 analysis and readopt the 2021 analysis with modifications
Uber FY2025 10-K: reclassification 'would require us to fundamentally change our business model'
H.R.1319 Modern Worker Empowerment Act reported amended (H. Rept. 119-505) and placed on the Union Calendar - statutory IC standard advancing in parallel

financial_linkage.detail: Consolidated FY2025 revenue $52.0B (XBRL). Mobility/Delivery driver economics are segment-reported; the incremental cost of employment classification is not disclosed by jurisdiction.
financial_linkage.gap: Per-driver cost delta under reclassification is not publicly disclosed; modeled estimates would require analyst-approved proxies (not used here).

cases.rationale: Uber's own disclosure makes the business linkage direct and Core: the supply model is the business. Federal process status is Proposal (a live NPRM to roll back the 2024 rule), not Adopted-and-static; treating a proposed rescission as settled law is the proposal trap this assessment avoids. Confidence is High because the rule documents and the company linkage are both primary sources. A parallel statutory track (H.R.1319, reported and on the Union Calendar) would codify a classification standard; both tracks point the same direction but neither is final.
gaps: State classification regimes (e.g. California Proposition 22 litigation, state minimum-earnings laws) are disclosed by Uber but state-level connectors are not built; the federal picture alone understates total classification exposure.

cases.title: Reciprocal tariff regime on imported goods (Executive Order 14257 amendments)
cases.sub_issue: reciprocal tariffs and import duties (US federal)

business_activity.name: US retail sale of imported general merchandise and groceries

cases.authority: Executive Office of the President (executive orders under IEEPA); HTSUS modifications administered by CBP/USTR
cases.policy_mechanism: Cost or tax: executive orders imposing additional ad valorem duties on goods of trading partners at rates set in annexes, modifying the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS), with scope adjustments tied to trade and security agreements

mechanism_chain.text: Executive orders published in the Federal Register impose additional ad valorem duties on goods of certain trading partners at annexed rates and modify the HTSUS, effective for goods entered for consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. EDT 7 days after the July/August 2025 order.

A September 2025 order modifies the annex of exempted goods and states that, except in rare circumstances, the reciprocal tariff scope will not be narrowed before conclusion of a final trade and security agreement with the partner.

As an import-reliant retailer, Walmart's cost of goods sold is exposed to these duties across sourcing countries; the company-level exposure (import share, vendor absorption, price pass-through) is not quantified in retrieved sources, so the magnitude is asserted at the regime level only.

events.description: Executive order 'Further Modifying the Reciprocal Tariff Rates' published in the Federal Register: additional ad valorem duties at Annex I rates in lieu of prior EO 14257 rates; HTSUS modified per Annex II, effective 7 days after the order

Executive order 'Modifying the Scope of Reciprocal Tariffs and Establishing Procedures to Implement Trade and Security Agreements' published: Annex II exemption list updated; scope narrowing tied to final agreements

financial_linkage.detail: Consolidated FY2026 revenue $713.2B (SEC EDGAR XBRL us-gaap:Revenues, 10-K filed 2026-03-13; fiscal year ended 2026-01-31). No company-specific import or tariff-cost figures in retrieved sources; the tariff rates and product scope are published only at the regime level (annexes).
financial_linkage.gap: Company-level exposure cannot be derived from regime-level annexes without Walmart sourcing/import data - labeled Unknown per the financial linkage ladder.

cases.rationale: The tariff regime itself is directly evidenced by two executive orders in the Federal Register and is in force. Exposure is rated Meaningful rather than Core because the company linkage is inferred, not direct: Walmart is a large import-reliant retailer, but no retrieved source quantifies its import share or tariff cost, and SEC EDGAR company filings are blocked from the build environment. Evidence confidence is Medium for the same reason - the policy facts are High-confidence; the company-specific exposure rests on inference.
gaps: SEC EDGAR 10-K full text for Walmart not yet snapshotted in this build - company tariff risk disclosure is pending, not absent. (EDGAR reachable via browser fetch; submissions and revenue concept retrieved.)
Senate LDA lobbying filings are likewise blocked (HTTP 403) - Walmart advocacy on trade policy is not covered in this build.

cases.title: SEC climate-related disclosure rules (adopted 2024, rescission proposed 2026)
cases.sub_issue: mandatory climate disclosure (US federal securities regulation)
cases.policy_mechanism: Disclosure mandate: climate-related information requirements in registration statements and annual reports

mechanism_chain.text: The SEC's climate disclosure amendments require registrants to provide climate-related information in registration statements and annual reports.
In June 2026 the SEC proposed to rescind those amendments, with comments due August 3, 2026.

For ExxonMobil the mechanism is a compliance-cost and litigation-risk question, not a market-access question; XOM's 10-K already flags mandatory disclosure and due-diligence requirements as a compliance-cost driver.

events.description: SEC proposes rescission of climate-related disclosure rules; comments due 2026-08-03
XOM FY2025 10-K flags mandatory disclosure and due-diligence requirements as compliance-cost drivers

financial_linkage.detail: Compliance-cost exposure only; no revenue linkage. Disclosure rules do not map to a revenue line.
financial_linkage.gap: None material for this mechanism; litigation status of the original 2024 rule (8th Circuit consolidation) is not covered by a court connector.

cases.rationale: On the emerging list because the operative fact is a proposed rescission, not a settled rulebook: the proposal trap applies in both directions (neither the 2024 rule's survival nor its rescission is certain). Business exposure is Limited - this changes reporting obligations, not operations. The original rule's court challenge is disclosed territory but outside current connector coverage, hence Material gaps.
gaps: No court connector for the consolidated litigation over the 2024 climate disclosure rule.
State and foreign disclosure regimes (California SB 253/261, EU CSRD) are not yet connected and may bind XOM regardless of the SEC outcome.

cases.title: Federal methane regulation of oil and gas operations (standards rollback plus methane-fee repeal)
cases.sub_issue: methane emissions standards and charges (US federal)

business_activity.name: US upstream oil and natural gas production operations

cases.authority: US Environmental Protection Agency / US Congress (Congressional Review Act)
cases.policy_mechanism: Emission standards compliance (CAA section 111, OOOOb/c) and a statutory per-ton methane charge (IRA section 136) - the charge rule was revoked under the CRA and standard deadlines are being extended and reconsidered

mechanism_chain.text: EPA's March 2024 oil and gas sector climate rule set performance standards and emissions guidelines; in July 2025 EPA took interim final action extending certain compliance deadlines.

The IRA Waste Emissions Charge ($900/ton methane in 2024 rising to $1,500/ton in 2026) was implemented by EPA in November 2024, then disapproved by Congress and removed from the CFR in May 2025 under the Congressional Review Act.

The direction of travel is deregulatory: near-term compliance cost and charge exposure for US upstream operations is falling, while the underlying CAA 111 framework and any future reconsideration remain live.

Oil and natural gas facilities are the nation's largest industrial source of methane, a greenhouse gas (GHG) that is 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide (CO2) and is responsible for approximately one third of all warming resulting from anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases.\1\ The three-part framework established by Congress in CAA section 136 addresses these emissions by: (1) directing the EPA to impose and collect a ``Waste Emissions Charge'' (WEC) on methane emissions from high-emitting and inefficient oil and gas operations; (2) directing the EPA to update subpart W of the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program to ensure accurate reporting of methane emissions by oil and natural gas facilities that is based on empirical data; and (3) providing over $1 billion in financial and technical assistance to assist the industry, States, and communities in deploying methane mitigation and monitoring solutions.

The WEC advances the reduction of methane emissions from the oil and gas sector by providing for sources covered under the CAA section 111 rules a set of emissions reduction incentives that are in effect until full implementation of oil and gas methane emissions standards promulgated by the EPA on March 8, 2024.
